name: Design a Data Quality Monitoring Platform
intent: Watch thousands of warehouse tables for late, missing, duplicated or drifting data, tell the right owner within minutes, and stop bad data from reaching dashboards and models, without scanning petabytes or waking people for nothing.
codeTitle: a seasonal volume check and a circuit breaker
finalIntro: One hourly load that arrives with two thirds of its rows missing, from the check to the page.
prompt: Design a platform that monitors the quality of 10,000 tables in a data warehouse. Teams declare checks on their tables: freshness, row volume, null rate, uniqueness and drift in the distribution of values. The platform learns what normal looks like, alerts the owner of the broken data and the owners of everything downstream, and can stop a bad load from flowing into reports and machine-learning features.
functional: Declare checks on a table as configuration: freshness, volume, null rate, uniqueness, value distribution, schema
Run checks on a schedule or when a load finishes, and keep the history of every result
Detect unusual values without a hand-set threshold, taking daily and weekly rhythms into account
Alert the owner of the table, and show which downstream tables, dashboards and models are affected
Stop a failing load from being published to consumers, and release it after a fix
Let owners mute, tune and give feedback on alerts
nonFunctional: A bad load is caught within minutes of landing, before the next consumer reads it
Checks add little cost: far less than the pipelines they watch
Fewer than a few false pages per owner per week, or people stop reading them
Handle about 300,000 check runs a day and stay up even when the warehouse is slow
Never lose the history of results, since baselines and audits depend on it
A failure of the monitor must not stop the pipelines, unless a check has said the data is bad

firstAttempt.text: Each team writes SQL assertions in its own cron job, such as select count(*) from orders where day = today, compares the number with a constant they picked, and sends an email when it is off. Nothing is shared and the dashboards simply read whatever is in the tables.
limits: Every check scans the table in full, so the quality jobs cost almost as much as the pipelines
A fixed threshold cannot fit a volume that is ten times higher at 3 pm than at 3 am, and ten times lower on Sunday
Every team reinvents the checks, and nobody can say which tables are covered
An email goes to whoever wrote the job, even when the broken table is an upstream one
Nothing stops the bad data: reports are already wrong by the time anyone reads the mail

steps.title: Declare checks as configuration, and run them in one engine
steps.problem: Hand-written SQL in cron jobs gives no shared vocabulary, no list of what is covered, and no common place to keep results.
steps.fix: Teams declare checks in a small file kept in Git next to the table: the table, the kind of check (freshness, volume, null rate of a column, uniqueness of a key, distribution of a column, expected schema), its schedule and its owner. A check engine reads the specs, turns each one into a query on the warehouse, runs it when the load finishes or on a timer, and writes a row to a result history: table, check, time, measured value, verdict. Because checks are data, the platform can answer which tables are covered, and a template can add the standard five checks to every new table.
steps.tradeoff: One format, review in pull requests and a measured coverage replace scattered scripts. The engine becomes a shared service that must be reliable, and a declarative language is less flexible than free SQL, so it needs an escape hatch for custom checks.

steps.title: Learn what normal looks like, hour by hour
steps.problem: A fixed threshold is wrong all the time: an order table loads 900 thousand rows at 3 pm, 60 thousand at 3 am and 40% of that on a weekend. Either the alert fires every night or it never fires for a real drop.
steps.fix: Compare each measurement with the same moment in earlier weeks. The baseline for Wednesday 14:00 is the median of the last four Wednesdays at 14:00, and its spread is the median absolute deviation (MAD), scaled by 1.48 so that it estimates a standard deviation, with a floor of a few percent of the median so that a very steady series does not alert on a rounding wobble. A value more than k spreads from the median is anomalous. The median and MAD are used instead of the mean and standard deviation because one past incident hardly moves them. Daily and weekly rhythm, and a trend over several weeks, can be added with a seasonal model, but the simple version already removes most false alarms.
steps.tradeoff: Alerts become specific to the table and the hour, and no one has to pick numbers. A new table has no history, so it starts with wide fixed limits and switches to the baseline after a few weeks, and holidays and launches look like anomalies unless they are annotated.

steps.title: Make checks cheap: metadata, increments and samples
steps.problem: Counting rows, nulls and distinct keys by reading every table in full, 300,000 times a day, would cost more than the pipelines being watched.
steps.fix: Use the cheapest source that can answer. Freshness and row counts come from table metadata, such as the last commit time and file statistics, with no data read at all. Heavier checks only read the newest partition, because yesterday's partition has not changed, and store a small summary (row count, null count, sketches for distinct counts, histogram bins) per partition so that history is never rescanned. Null rate and distribution drift run on a one percent sample of that partition, which gives a rate accurate to a fraction of a percent. Uniqueness needs the full partition, or a sketch, since a sample can miss duplicates.
steps.tradeoff: The cost drops by several orders of magnitude, and a bad load is seen in minutes, since only the new partition is read. A sampled check can miss a rare problem, such as one bad row in a million, so the checks that must be exact, like uniqueness of a key, are still full scans of just the new partition.

steps.title: Route alerts by lineage and ownership
steps.problem: When an upstream table breaks, forty tables below it fail their checks too, and forty teams are paged for a problem that belongs to one of them.
steps.fix: Keep a lineage graph of which tables feed which, built from the SQL the pipelines run and from the orchestrator, and an ownership record for each table. When checks fail, the router walks the graph upstream to find the most upstream failing table, which is the likely root cause, pages only its owner, and attaches the list of impacted downstream tables, dashboards and models, with their owners, as information. The others get one grouped notice, and alerts carry the table, the check, the measured value, the expected range and a link to the run.
steps.tradeoff: One page replaces forty and it goes to the people who can fix it, and consumers learn their data is suspect before they find out for themselves. The lineage graph must be kept current, and a wrong or missing edge sends the page to the wrong team or hides an impact.

steps.title: Stop bad data with a circuit breaker and quarantine
steps.problem: Alerts arrive after the load has been published, and a dashboard that shows half the day's orders is already wrong, and has already been read.
steps.fix: Load into a staging area first, run the blocking checks on it, and only then publish (write, audit, publish). The pipeline asks a circuit breaker whether the table is healthy. A failing check puts the partition in a quarantine area instead of publishing it, and consumers keep reading the last good version. After a second failing load in a row the breaker opens for the table, so downstream jobs pause instead of each reading stale data on a schedule, and it closes after several clean loads or when an owner releases or replays the partition. Each check is marked as blocking or informational, so only the ones that are trusted can stop a pipeline.
steps.tradeoff: Wrong numbers no longer reach consumers, and a replay is possible since the bad partition is kept. Consumers see stale but correct data during an incident, and a check that is wrong can now stop the business, which is why new checks start in warn-only mode.

steps.title: Tune the noise with feedback and budgets
steps.problem: A platform that cries wolf is muted within a month, and then it catches nothing.
steps.fix: Every alert has buttons: real, not a problem, expected (a holiday or a launch). The tuning service records them, widens the sensitivity for checks that are often marked not a problem and tightens it for checks that miss real incidents. A check can be muted for a window, and calendar annotations tell the baseline about holidays. Related alerts within a few minutes are merged into one page, repeats are suppressed, and each owner has a page budget, such as three a week, with a report on which checks use it up. New checks run in warn-only mode for two weeks before they can page or block.
steps.tradeoff: Pages that do reach people are trusted, and the rules improve with use. Automatic widening can hide a real slow decline, so changes are logged, bounded and reviewed, and a few seeded test incidents are replayed regularly to confirm that the checks still catch them.

failures.scenario: The check engine or the warehouse is down or slow
failures.impact: Checks do not run, so a bad load could be published, or if every unfinished check blocks, all pipelines stop.
failures.answer: Each check has a timeout, and the policy for a missing result is chosen per table: fail open and publish with an alert that the monitor itself is late for ordinary tables, fail closed and hold the partition for the few critical ones. The platform's own freshness is watched by an independent heartbeat check, and check queries run in a separate warehouse queue so they cannot slow the pipelines.

failures.scenario: A holiday or a product launch changes the volume on purpose
failures.impact: The seasonal baseline sees a normal week, so a sale that triples orders or a holiday that halves them pages many teams.
failures.answer: Owners and the calendar annotate the event, and the baseline either widens for those hours or compares with the same event last year. The first alert is marked expected with one click, which is remembered, and a spike that is flagged is excluded from future baselines when it was wrong, so the median stays clean.

failures.scenario: An upstream outage makes hundreds of checks fail at once
failures.impact: Owners of every downstream table get paged, the on-call channel floods, and the real cause is buried.
failures.answer: The router finds the most upstream failing table through lineage and pages its owner once, and downstream failures become a grouped notice with the impact list. During the storm, notifications are rate limited per team, and the breaker holds all downstream loads so that nothing computes on bad inputs.

failures.scenario: A bad week gets into the baseline
failures.impact: If a broken load was published and counted, next month's baseline treats the broken value as normal, and the same fault no longer alerts.
failures.answer: Baselines use the median and MAD, so one bad week among four hardly moves them, and measurements from failed or quarantined partitions are flagged and left out of the baseline altogether. A weekly comparison against a slower, longer baseline reports when the two disagree, which catches a slow decline that every short baseline absorbs.

alternatives.title: How normal is defined

options.name: A fixed threshold
options.pro: Trivial to explain and to implement
options.con: Wrong at some hours of every day, so it either spams or sleeps

options.name: Same hour of the week, median and MAD
options.pro: Handles daily and weekly rhythm, robust to past incidents, needs no tuning knob except k
options.con: Needs a few weeks of history and notices holidays late

options.name: A forecasting model per metric
options.pro: Captures trends, several seasons and holidays
options.con: Costly to train for tens of thousands of series, and harder to explain to the owner who is paged

alternatives.pick: The seasonal median and MAD for most checks, a forecasting model only for the few high-value tables.

alternatives.title: Where checks run

options.name: Queries pushed down to the warehouse
options.pro: No data movement, and the warehouse does the work in parallel
options.con: Uses warehouse capacity that must be isolated from the pipelines

options.name: A separate engine that reads the data
options.pro: Independent of the warehouse and flexible
options.con: Moves data out, which is slow, costly and a governance concern

options.name: Assertions inside the pipeline code
options.pro: Runs exactly when the data is made, and can block in the same step
options.con: Hard to cover tables that others produce, and each team codes its own

alternatives.pick: Pushdown queries from the central engine, with in-pipeline assertions for the blocking checks of the critical tables.

alternatives.title: What a failing check does

options.name: Alert only
options.pro: Safe: it can never stop a pipeline
options.con: The bad data is already published and read

options.name: Write, audit, publish with a circuit breaker
options.pro: Consumers never see a failing partition and keep the last good data
options.con: A wrong check blocks the business, so it needs a trust process

options.name: Quarantine only the bad rows
options.con: Only works for row-level rules, and a table with missing rows is now incomplete without saying so

alternatives.pick: Alert only for new checks, then block with a breaker once a check has proven itself. Row-level quarantine for row-level rules such as a null key.

alternatives.title: Where lineage comes from

options.name: Parsed from the SQL and jobs
options.pro: Automatic and complete for what is parsed
options.con: Dynamic SQL and code transformations are missed or guessed

options.name: Emitted by the orchestrator at run time
options.pro: What actually ran, with no guessing
options.con: Only covers the tools that emit it

options.name: Entered by hand
options.pro: Captures what no tool sees, such as a dashboard owner

alternatives.pick: Parsed and emitted lineage for tables, with hand-entered owners and consumers at the edges.

roles.label: Owners
roles.description: The teams that are paged and read the impact.

roles.label: Pipeline
roles.description: The orchestrator that loads and publishes tables.

roles.label: Checks
roles.description: The check engine, sampler, breaker and tuning.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Tables, specs, result history, baselines and lineage.
